overview.headline: Plutonium isotopes, radioactivity, decay and reactor fuel uses

keyPoints.point: Plutonium is a radioactive metal created in a reactor when uranium atoms absorb neutrons.
keyPoints.quote: Plutonium is created in a reactor when uranium atoms absorb neutrons.

keyPoints.point: Plutonium also emits neutrons, beta particles and gamma rays in addition to other radiation.
keyPoints.quote: It also emits neutrons, beta particles and gamma rays.

keyPoints.point: Substances with shorter half-lives decay more quickly and emit more energetic radioactivity.
keyPoints.quote: Substances with shorter half-lives decay more quickly than those with longer half-lives, so they emit more energetic radioactivity.

keyPoints.point: Spent nuclear fuel from reactors still contains plutonium that stays in the fuel.
keyPoints.quote: Spent nuclear fuel from U.S. reactors contains about 1 percent plutonium by weight.

keyTerms.gloss: nearly all man-made metal containing plutonium
radioactive metallic element made in reactors
keyTerms.quote: Plutonium is a radioactive metallic element with the atomic number 94.

keyTerms.gloss: particles emitted with beta particles and gamma rays
keyTerms.quote: It also emits neutrons, beta particles and gamma rays.

keyTerms.gloss: time for substances to decay with energetic radioactivity
keyTerms.quote: Substances with shorter half-lives decay more quickly than those with longer half-lives, so they emit more energetic radioactivity.

keyTerms.gloss: radioactive forms that transform when they decay
keyTerms.quote: Like any radioactive isotopes, plutonium isotopes transform when they decay.

keyTerms.gloss: process using chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium
keyTerms.quote: This process, known as reprocessing, uses chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium and other fission products.

keyTerms.gloss: mixed oxide produced from plutonium oxide and uranium oxide
keyTerms.quote: Once separated, plutonium oxide can be mixed with uranium oxide to produce mixed oxide or MOX fuel.
